items.title: Marcellus wells (deviated), West Virginia
items.description: 2,536 permitted Marcellus wells with a deviated or horizontal bore, the shape gas development takes in this part of the state. Shown alongside the water quality network so a reader can judge for themselves whether the two line up. Source: WV Geological and Economic Survey, 2020-02-06, redistributed by WVU GIS Technical Center.

items.title: West Virginia water quality, 1995 to 2019
items.description: Twenty-five years of water quality monitoring across West Virginia's north-central gas counties: 1,175 sites and 285,788 individual measurements, each carrying the published drinking water limit for what it measured. Health-based limits and aesthetic ones are kept apart, because an iron reading that stains laundry and an arsenic reading that does not are not the same finding. Source: West Virginia GIS Technical Center / West Virginia University, EPA water quality project (data.wvgis.wvu.edu/pub/project/epa_wq), file WQandWell_Data_042020.gdb dated 2020-04-09. Compiled by Maneesh Sharma and colleagues from WVDEP, USGS and partner monitoring programmes.

items.title: West Virginia water quality network
items.description: Monitoring sites coloured by the worst drinking water standard they have ever breached, over Marcellus wells for context. Health based limits are kept visually distinct from aesthetic ones: iron that stains a sink and arsenic that does not are not the same finding. Individual measurements are present but switched off, because 285,788 readings stacked on 1,175 locations is a smear until you are zoomed in.

items.title: Twenty-five years of West Virginia water quality
items.description: 1,175 monitoring sites and 285,788 measurements from the gas counties of north-central West Virginia, 1995 to 2019, each reading compared to its published drinking water limit. The counters and charts follow the map: pan or zoom and every number re-answers for what is on screen. Source: WVU GIS Technical Center / EPA water quality project.

config.title: Sites over the limit, by what was measured
config.description: Distinct SITES, not readings: one creek sampled monthly for a decade is one site. Ochre is an aesthetic standard (taste, odour, staining); red is a health-based one. Click a bar to show those sites on the map. Iron, aluminium and manganese are the signature of acid mine drainage. Barium and radium would indicate gas brine, and are near zero.

config.title: Has anyone been looking? (statewide)
config.description: Distinct sites sampled each year, across the whole study area. This one does not follow the map: the story is the twenty-five year arc, and at most zoom levels the yearly counts are too thin to show it. Monitoring peaked at 325 sites in 2010 and had fallen to 53 by 2018.

config.title: How much iron, actually
config.description: Every iron reading, by concentration. The limit is a secondary standard: staining and taste, not health. Ranges widen because the values span four orders of magnitude.

config.markdown:
### What this shows

Every water quality measurement taken at 1,175 sites across West
Virginia's north-central gas counties between 1995 and 2019, compared
to the published drinking water limit for what was measured.

### The finding

In counties chosen for study **because** of Marcellus gas development,
the water quality problem the data actually shows is **iron,
aluminium, manganese and acidity**. That is the signature of acid mine
drainage from a century of coal, not of gas brine. Iron is over its
limit at 862 of the 982 sites where it was measured; aluminium at 692
of 865; manganese at 613 of 792.

The parameters that would indicate produced water from gas operations
are almost never over their limits: barium at 1 site of 239, chloride
at 54 of 832, radium-226 and radium-228 at none at all.

### Two things that must travel with that

**The gas indicators were measured far less.** Barium was tested at
239 sites against iron's 982; radium at 30; gross uranium at 30. You
cannot conclude much from 30 sites, and a green zero should not be
read as an all-clear.

**These are mostly streams.** Surface water dilutes. The groundwater
that people actually drink from private wells is a small slice of this
dataset.

### Health limits versus aesthetic ones

A primary standard is health based. A secondary standard is about
taste, odour and staining. Iron, manganese, aluminium, sulfate,
chloride, total dissolved solids and pH are **secondary**: 1,003 sites
exceed one, and that mostly means discoloured water and stained
fixtures. Only **3 sites** have ever exceeded a health-based limit.
The two are never added together here.

### Has anyone been looking

Monitoring peaked at 325 sites in 2010 and had fallen to 53 by 2018.
**861 of the 1,175 sites have not been sampled since 2015.** For many
people the most useful thing this map can tell them is that nobody has
measured anything near them in a decade.

### Source

West Virginia GIS Technical Center / West Virginia University, EPA
water quality project, file `WQandWell_Data_042020.gdb` dated
2020-04-09, compiled from WVDEP, USGS and partner monitoring
programmes. Marcellus wells from the WV Geological and Economic
Survey, 2020-02-06. Redistributed as-is with attribution; no license
asserted by the publishers.

Contaminant limits are the ones published in the source's own
parameter table. Where a standard is a range (pH 6.5 to 8.5,
aluminium 0.05 to 0.2 mg/L) the operative bound is used.

items.title: Elkins buildings with lidar heights
items.description: Every mapped building in and around Elkins, West Virginia, carrying a height measured from 2018 lidar. The lidar is not building-classified, so heights are not read from the file: they are the 90th percentile of a max-return surface minus a ground surface, sampled inside each footprint. The percentile rather than the maximum because footprints in a small town abut tree canopy and one overhanging limb should not decide how tall a building is. Treat the numbers as good relative heights rather than survey measurements. Footprints too small to cover a raster cell keep a nominal 4 m and are marked 'assumed' so they can be told apart. Built to demonstrate 3D extrusion on open data. Building footprints: © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL. Heights derived from public-domain 2018 lidar.

items.title: Elkins in 3D (map)
items.description: Every mapped building in Elkins, West Virginia, standing at a height measured from 2018 lidar rather than guessed. Tilt and rotate to read the town's shape: the courthouse block and the Davis and Elkins campus rise out of a two-storey downtown. Colour repeats the height so the map still reads looking straight down. Built entirely from open data and the portal's own tools. The lidar hillshade raster is not included in this sample (about 56 MB).
